definition: A radar that asks each aircraft a radio question and reads the answer sent back by its transponder: an identity code and the altitude. It needs the aircraft to cooperate.
The interrogation is the radar's question: a few short pulses on 1030 MHz. The reply is the transponder's answer: a train of pulses on 1090 MHz.
The SSR question "who are you?". The transponder answers with its four-digit squawk code. P1 and P3 are 8 microseconds apart.
The SSR question "how high are you?". The transponder answers with its pressure altitude in 100 ft steps. P1 and P3 are 21 microseconds apart.
Selective SSR: every aircraft has its own 24-bit address, and the radar calls one aircraft at a time by that address. Replies carry more data, such as the callsign.
The first and last pulses of an SSR reply, exactly 20.3 microseconds apart. They tell the radar where a reply starts and ends; the code pulses sit between them.
Special position identification: an extra pulse after F2 that the transponder adds for about 18 seconds when the pilot presses IDENT, so the controller can pick out that aircraft.
Weak radio energy an antenna sends in directions other than its main beam. Close to the radar, a side lobe can still be strong enough to trigger a transponder.

The radar sends a second pulse, P2, from an antenna that radiates equally in all directions. In the main beam P1 is much stronger than P2; in a side lobe P2 is stronger, so the transponder knows not to answer.
Two aircraft close together (less than about 1.7 NM apart in distance from the radar) answer the same Mode A/C question and their reply pulses overlap, so the codes get mixed up.
False Replies Unsynchronized In Time: answers that other radars triggered. They reach your receiver at random moments, so they appear at random distances.
A filter that keeps a reply only if another reply turns up at the same distance on the next questions. Real aircraft pass the test; random FRUIT does not.
A number unique to each aircraft, assigned by its country of registration, written as six hexadecimal digits such as 8A01A1. Mode S and ADS-B use it to tell aircraft apart.
A Mode S radar first sends an all-call ("everyone new, tell me your address"), then calls each aircraft by name with a roll-call. After it is known, an aircraft stops answering all-calls (lockout).
The way Mode C packs altitude into the 12 reply pulses. Neighbouring altitudes differ in exactly one pulse, so a reading taken mid-change is never far wrong.
Altitude worked out from air pressure with the standard setting of 1013.25 hPa. Mode C always reports it, so every aircraft is measured the same way.
Codes with a fixed meaning everywhere: 7500 unlawful interference (hijack), 7600 radio failure, 7700 emergency. The controller's screen shows them in words.
Mode S radars reading extra data from the aircraft's own systems, such as the altitude set on the autopilot, heading and speed. The data sits in numbered registers called BDS.
The part of the radar that groups the many replies from one pass of the beam into a single target report (a plot) with one position, code and altitude.
The weakest question a transponder answers, about −74 dBm. Weaker interrogations are ignored.
A way for a radar to measure the direction of a single reply very precisely by comparing two antenna patterns at once. It lets Mode S work with only one or two replies per turn.
When side lobes are not suppressed, an aircraft close to the radar answers in many directions and shows as a ring or arcs of false targets around the radar.
